en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on the Defeats (Pārājikakaṇḍa)
4. The Fourth Pārājika Training Rule At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Forest in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus who were friends and associates entered the rains retreat on the bank of the river Vaggumudā.
Now at that time, the Vajjis were suffering from a famine; there was a scarcity of food, crops had withered, bones lay bleaching, and people lived by gleaning stalks;
it was not easy to subsist by gathering gleanings. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:

“At present, the Vajjis are suffering from a famine; there is a scarcity of food, crops have withered, bones lie bleaching, and people live by gleaning stalks; it is not easy to subsist by gathering gleanings.”
"By what means indeed might we dwell together in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, spending the rains comfortably and not being distressed for alms?
Some said this:
“Come, friends, let us undertake work for householders;
thus they will think to give to us.
In this way we shall dwell together in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, and spend the rains comfortably.”
"And we shall not be exhausted by seeking alms.
Some said this:
"Enough, friends; why persist in attending to the work of householders?"
"Come, friends, let us carry messages for householders;
thus they will think to give to us.
In this way, being united, in harmony, and without dispute, we shall spend the rains retreat in comfort."
"And we shall not be exhausted by the search for alms-food.
Some said this:
"Enough, friends; what is the use of being intent upon the work of householders?"
"What is the use of acting as a messenger for householders by force?
Come, friends, let us speak in praise of one another's superhuman states among the householders:
'Such-and-such a bhikkhu is an attainer of the first jhāna;'"
Such-and-such a bhikkhu is an attainer of the second jhāna;
such-and-such a bhikkhu is an attainer of the third jhāna;
such-and-such a bhikkhu is an attainer of the fourth jhāna.
Such-and-such a bhikkhu is a stream-enterer;
such-and-such a bhikkhu is a once-returner;
such-and-such a bhikkhu is a non-returner.
“Such-and-such a bhikkhu is an arahant;
such-and-such a bhikkhu is one possessed of the three knowledges;
such-and-such a bhikkhu is one possessed of the six direct knowledges.”
"In this way they will think to give to us.
In this way we shall dwell together in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, spending the rains comfortably and not being distressed for lack of almsfood."
“Indeed, friends, it is better that we speak in praise of one another’s superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) as householders.
Then those bhikkhus spoke in praise of one another’s superhuman states among the householders:
“Such-and-such a bhikkhu is an attainer of the first jhāna... [and so on]...”
“Such-and-such a bhikkhu possesses the sixfold direct knowledge.
Then those people thought:
“It is indeed a gain for us, it is truly well-gained for us, that such bhikkhus have entered the rains residence with us!”
"Indeed, never before have we had such bhikkhus enter the rains retreat as these bhikkhus who are virtuous and of lovely character.

Thinking thus, they do not consume such food themselves; rather, they give it to their parents, they give it to their wives and children, they give it to their slaves, laborers, and servants, they give it to their friends and companions, and they give it to their kinsmen and blood relations—just the kind of food they give to the bhikkhus.
They themselves eat, taste, and drink such kinds of solid foods, soft foods, and drinks;

they give them to their mother and father, they give them to their children and wives, they give them to their slaves, laborers, and servants, they give them to their friends and colleagues, and they give them to their kinsmen and blood relations—
just as the kinds they give to the bhikkhus.
Then those monks became handsome, with bright faculties, serene facial complexions, and clear skin.
Now it is the custom for monks who have completed the rains retreat to approach the Blessed One to see him.
So, at the end of the three months after completing the rains retreat, those monks put their lodgings in order, took their bowls and robes, and set out for Vesālī.
Gradually, they approached Vesālī, the Great Wood, the Gabled Hall, and where the Blessed One was. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Now at that time, the monks who had completed the rains retreat in various directions were thin, coarse, discolored, pale and sallow, with their limbs covered in visible veins;
but the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River were handsome, with bright faculties, clear complexions, and a serene skin tone.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One said this to the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River:
"Monks, I hope you are bearing up; I hope you are getting along?"
“I hope you have spent the rains residence in harmony, in mutual agreement, without dispute, living at ease and not distressed for lack of almsfood?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One.
We have spent the rains residence in harmony, venerable sir, in mutual agreement, without dispute, living at ease and not distressed for lack of almsfood.”
Tathāgatas ask even though they know; they do not ask even though they know...
Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, question the bhikkhus for two reasons: "Either we shall teach the Dhamma, or we shall lay down a training rule for the disciples.
Then the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhus dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River:
“But how, monks, did you dwell in harmony, in mutual agreement, without dispute, comfortably during the rains retreat, and without being distressed for lack of almsfood?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“But is it true, monks, that this actually happened?”
“It was not true, Blessed One,” they said.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unseemly, foolish men, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
"How can you, foolish men, for the sake of your bellies, speak in praise of one another’s superhuman states to householders?

It would be better for you, foolish men, to have your bellies cut open with a sharp butcher’s knife than to speak in praise of one another’s superhuman states to householders for the sake of your bellies. Why is that?"
For on that account, foolish men, one might meet death or suffering amounting to death;
yet for that reason alone, with the breakup of the body after death, one would not be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, or hell.
But on this account, foolish men, with the breakup of the body after death, one would indeed be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, or hell.
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
‘Monks, there are these five great thieves found existing in the world.’”
What are the five?
Here, monks, it occurs to a certain great thief:
“When indeed shall I wander through villages, market towns, and royal capitals surrounded by a hundred or a thousand [followers]?”
"Killing, causing to kill, mutilating, causing to mutilate, cooking, causing to cook.

Then, at a later time, surrounded by a hundred or a thousand followers, he wanders through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, killing, causing to kill, mutilating, causing to mutilate, cooking, and causing to cook.
In the same way, monks, it occurs to a certain evil monk here:
‘When indeed shall I wander on tour through villages, market towns, and royal capitals surrounded by a retinue of a hundred or a thousand,

honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by both householders and those who have gone forth, and receiving robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick? Then, at a later time,
surrounded by a retinue of a hundred or a thousand, he wanders on tour through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
He lives honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated by both householders and those who have gone forth,
and he is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, monks, is the first great thief existing and found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, conceals it within himself.
This, monks, is the second great thief existing and found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain wicked monk groundlessly accuses a pure practitioner of holy life who is living a perfectly pure holy life of unchastity.
This, monks, is the third great thief existing and found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here some evil bhikkhu takes those things belonging to the Saṅgha that are heavy goods and heavy requisites, namely:
a monastery or a monastery site, a dwelling or a dwelling site, a bed, a bench, a mattress, a pillow, a bronze cauldron, or a bronze bowl.
Iron vessels, iron cauldrons, axes, hatchets, adzes, spades, pickaxes, creepers, bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass,
grass, clay, wooden articles, and earthenware— by means of these,
he favors and gratifies the householder.
This, monks, is the fourth great thief found existing in the world.

In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, this is the foremost great thief: one who claims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state. And why is that?
“Monks, you have eaten the alms of the country by means of theft.
He who represents himself as one thing while being quite another;
That which he has eaten by theft is like the winnings of a gambler;
many are those with saffron robes around their necks.
Those of evil nature, unrestrained,
through their wicked deeds,
they are reborn in hell.
Better it would be to eat a red-hot iron ball,
glowing like a crest of fire,
than that one who is immoral should eat [the alms of the faithful].
"Unrestrained, he consumes the alms of the country.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the bhikkhus from Vaggumudā in many ways for their difficulty in supporting themselves and their difficulty in being nourished...
"And furthermore, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule thus:"
“Whatever bhikkhu, without direct knowledge, should claim for himself a superhuman state, a state of noble knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, saying: ‘Thus I know;

thus I see’—and then at a later time, whether being questioned or not being questioned, being one who has fallen into that offense and desiring purification, should say: ‘Friends, I said I knew when I did not know; I said I saw when I did not see;
it was empty, it was false, it was mere chatter’—this too is an offense entailing expulsion, one who is no longer in communion.”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.

Now at that time, a number of monks—perceiving what had not been seen as seen, perceiving what had not been attained as attained, perceiving what had not been reached as reached, and perceiving what had not been realized as realized—declared final knowledge out of overestimation.
At a later time, their minds inclined toward lust, their minds inclined toward hatred, and their minds inclined toward delusion.
They felt remorse, thinking:
"A training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One.

Yet we, regarding what was not seen as seen, what was not attained as attained, what was not reached as reached, and what was not realized as realized, have declared final knowledge out of overweening pride."
“Could it be that we have committed an offense entailing defeat?
They reported this matter to the Venerable Ānanda,
and the Venerable Ānanda reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Ānanda, those bhikkhus who perceive what has not been seen as seen, what has not been attained as attained, what has not been reached as reached, and what has not been realized as realized, and who on account of overweening pride declare final knowledge—
that is indeed outside of the proper course.
“And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:”
“Whatever monk, without direct knowledge, should claim for himself a superhuman state, a state of noble wisdom and insight, saying: ‘Thus I know;

thus I see’—and then, at a later time, whether being questioned or not being questioned, being guilty and desiring purification, should say: ‘Friends, I said I knew when I did not know; I said I saw when I did not see; I spoke empty falsehood’—except through overestimation [of oneself].”
“This too is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
“But whoever” means whoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Without having known":
Not knowing and not seeing the non-existent, the unreal, and the non-occurrent wholesome quality within oneself, one thinks: "I have a wholesome quality.
What is called a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) consists of:

jhāna, liberation (*vimokkha*), concentration (*samādhi*), attainment (*samāpatti*), knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), the cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*), the realization of the fruit (*phalasacchikiriyā*), the abandoning of defilements (*kilesappahāna*), freedom from hindrances (*vinīvaraṇatā*), and delight in empty dwellings (*suññāgāre abhirati*).
"Leading back to oneself" means that one brings those wholesome states to oneself, or brings oneself to those wholesome states.
"Knowledge" means...
The three true knowledges.
As for "vision":
that which is knowledge is vision, and that which is vision is knowledge.
"Should address" means she should inform a woman or a man, a householder or one who has gone forth, saying:
"Thus I know; thus I see."
"I know these states, I see these states; these states exist in me, and I am manifest in these states.
Then, at a later time—meaning when that moment, that instant, that brief duration during which the practice was habitual has passed.
"Being cross-examined regarding" means:
while being cross-examined concerning that very matter which has been admitted—"What have you realized? [he says:]...
How was it attained by you?
When was it attained by you?
Where was it attained by you?
"Which defilements have been abandoned by you,
and of which phenomena are you a possessor?"—
thus he was not pressed for an answer.
"Being spoken to by no one.

"One who has committed an offense" means that, being of evil desire and overcome by longing, having falsely claimed a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, he has committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika).
“Desirous of purification” means:
one who wishes to be a householder, or wishes to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or wishes to be a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), or wishes to be a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).
“Friend, not knowing, I said ‘I know’; not seeing, I said ‘I see’.”
"I do not know these things; I do not see these things; these things do not exist in me; nor am I manifest in these things.
Thus he speaks empty and false words:
"What I have spoken is empty; what I have spoken is false; what I have spoken is unreal; what I have spoken was said by one who does not know."
"Apart from overestimation" means excluding overestimation.
"This too" [is so].
It is said with reference to the former [offense].
"He becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense" means:
just as a palmyra tree whose crown has been cut off is incapable of further growth; so too is he.
In the same way, a bhikkhu who is of evil desires and overcome by desire, having falsely claimed a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, becomes one who is not a recluse, not a son of the Sakyan.
Therefore it is said: "He is one who has committed a pārājika offense.
He is no longer in communion.
“Living together” means performing formal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and training under the same rules—this is what is called living together.
He does not have that with him; therefore it is called “not living together.
“Superhuman states” means:

Meditative absorption (jhāna), liberation (vimokkha), concentration (samādhi), attainment (samāpatti), knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana), development of the path (maggabhāvanā), realization of the fruit (phalasacchikiriyā), the abandoning of defilements (kilesappahāna), freedom from hindrances (vinīvaraṇatā), and delight in an empty dwelling (suññāgāre abhirati).
As for "meditative absorption": it is the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna.
"Deliverance" refers to the void deliverance, the signless deliverance, and the desireless deliverance.
"Concentration" refers to—
The emptiness concentration, the signless concentration, and the desireless concentration.
As for "attainments," they are the emptiness attainment, the signless attainment, and the desireless attainment.
"Knowledge and vision" refers to the three true knowledges.
"Development of the path" refers to...
The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

“Realization of the fruits” means the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the realization of the fruit of once-returning, the realization of the fruit of non-returning, and the realization of arhatship.
The abandoning of defilements means the abandoning of lust, the abandoning of hatred, and the abandoning of delusion.
"The mind being free from hindrances" means:
The mind is unobstructed from lust, the mind is unobstructed from hatred, the mind is unobstructed from delusion.
"Delighting in an empty place" means delighting in an empty place by means of the first jhāna.
By means of the second jhāna, there is delight in an empty dwelling;
by means of the third jhāna, there is delight in an empty dwelling;
by means of the fourth jhāna, there is delight in an empty dwelling.
If one speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," in three ways, there is an offense entailing defeat:
before, he thinks, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
When he has spoken, it occurs to him: "I have spoken falsely.
For one who speaks a deliberate lie by saying, "I attained the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)—previously, it occurred to him: "I will speak falsely."
While speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood," and after having spoken,
he thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me," having set aside his own view.
For one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna by way of five factors," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika):
before speaking, he thinks, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
If, having set aside his view and set aside his preference, he thinks, "A falsehood was spoken by me," and he says,
"I have attained the first jhāna," then for one who speaks such a conscious lie, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in six ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference,
and having set aside one's inclination.
For one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "We have attained the first jhāna through the seven modes," there is an offense entailing defeat:
before he speaks, he thinks, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
When one who has spoken thinks, "I have spoken falsely," while setting aside his own view and setting aside his own conviction;
Having set aside one's preference,
having set aside one's disposition:
for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," in three ways, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
For one who speaks a conscious lie, thinking, "I shall attain the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)—
namely, when he first thinks, "I will speak a lie," and while speaking,
he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
If, having set aside his own view, he says of what was spoken, "I spoke falsely," or if he speaks a conscious lie,
saying, "I attained the first jhāna by means of five factors," he commits an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely";
after having spoken, one thinks, "Falsely have I spoken."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference:
for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I attain the first jhāna in six ways," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely";
after having spoken, one thinks, "Falsely have I spoken."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference,
having set aside one's inclination.
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I am attaining the first jhāna through the seven modes," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika):
before speaking, he thinks, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
When one who has spoken thinks, "I have spoken falsely," having set aside his view and having set aside his preference.
Having set aside his inclination,
having set aside his disposition,
if he says, "I have attained the first jhāna," while being fully aware that this is a lie, he commits an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in three ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
For one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in four ways:
before speaking he thinks, "I will speak a lie"; while speaking he thinks, "I am speaking a lie";
[and after speaking he thinks, "I have spoken a lie"].
If, having set aside his own view, he thinks, "I have spoken falsely," and he speaks knowingly a lie,
saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," he commits an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) for five reasons.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside his own view,
having set aside his own conviction:
for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in six ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference,
having set aside one's inclination.
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna through seven modes," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika):
before speaking, he thinks, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
When one who has spoken thinks, "I have spoken falsely," having set aside his view and having set aside his conviction.
Having set aside one's preference,
having set aside one's disposition,
if one speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I am an attainer of the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in three ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," when one has not, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika):
previously, one thinks, "I will speak a lie," and while speaking,
one thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
If, having set aside his own view, he thinks, "I have spoken falsely," and speaks a conscious lie,
saying, "I am an attainer of the first jhāna" in five ways, he commits an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference:
for one who speaks a conscious lie, saying "I am an attainer of the first jhāna" when one is not, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in six ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference,
having set aside one's inclination.
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have attained the first jhāna," when one has not attained it in its seven aspects, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika):
before speaking, the thought occurs, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, the thought occurs, "I am speaking a lie."
When one who has spoken thinks, "I have spoken falsely," while setting aside his own view and setting aside his own preference,
[he understands it as such].
Having set aside one’s preference,
having set aside one’s intention;
if one speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have mastery over the first jhāna" in three ways, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak falsely";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking falsely";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "I have spoken falsely."
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have mastery over the first jhāna," there is an offense of defeat (pārājika) for one who has four factors:
prior to speaking, the thought occurs, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, the thought occurs, "I am speaking a lie."
If, having set aside his own view, he thinks, "I have spoken falsely," and speaks intentional falsehood,
saying, "I have mastery over the first jhāna" in five ways, he commits an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's own view,
having set aside one's own preference:
if one speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have mastery over the first jhāna" in six ways, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference,
having set aside one's inclination.
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have mastery over the first jhāna through its seven aspects," there is an offense of defeat (pārājika):
before speaking, he thinks, "I will speak a lie";
while speaking, he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
When one who has spoken thinks,
"I have spoken falsely," while setting aside his view and setting aside his preference.
Having set aside one's inclination,
having set aside one's disposition,
for one who speaks a deliberate lie, saying, "I have realized the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in three ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have realized the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) for one who,
prior to speaking, thinks, "I will speak a lie," and while speaking,
thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
If, having set aside his own view, he thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me," and speaks a conscious lie,
saying, "I have realized the first jhāna through five modes," he commits an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one’s view,
having set aside one’s preference:
for one who speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have realized the first jhāna," there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) in six ways.
Before speaking, one thinks, "I will speak a falsehood";
while speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a falsehood";
and after having spoken, one thinks, "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
Having set aside one's view,
having set aside one's preference,
and having set aside one's inclination.
If one speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I have realized the first jhāna through the seven modes," there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*):
previously he thinks, "I will speak a lie," and while speaking,
he thinks, "I am speaking a lie."
When one who has spoken thinks, "I have spoken falsely," while setting aside his own view and setting aside his own conviction,
[he reflects thus].
Setting aside one's preference,
setting aside one's disposition.
